tasks.assumptions: Fictional western Canadian Class 2 water plant case: steady plant flow unless noted, archived plant and laboratory records available for review, and provincial drinking water requirements and the Guidelines for Canadian Drinking Water Quality apply in general terms.

evidence.label: The rapid mix motor current reads zero and the mixer shaft is not turning, although its run light is on.
Alum is being fed at the normal rate into the rapid mix chamber.
Jar tests mixed vigorously for one minute form uniform good floc at the plant dose.
Basin samples taken across the chamber vary widely, from well flocculated to almost raw.
Raw water quality and the flocculator paddles are normal.

inference.prompt: Which explanation is best supported by the observations?

options.label: The alum dose is too low for the raw water
The flocculator speed is too high and is shearing floc
The rapid mixer has failed, so coagulant is not dispersed through the raw water
Raw alkalinity is too low for coagulation

inference.explanation: The mixer is not turning, samples vary from treated to almost raw across the chamber, and vigorous mixing in a jar fixes the result at the same dose. Dose, shear and alkalinity do not explain untreated pockets beside good floc.

nextClue.prompt: Which archived record best confirms when the rapid mixer stopped?

options.label: Archived motor current trend and run status history for the rapid mixer
Archived jar test results from last month
Archived settled turbidity monthly summary

nextClue.explanation: Archived motor current trend and run status history for the rapid mixer directly records the condition behind the keyed explanation over time, so it best confirms it against the alternatives.

clueText.nc-a: Current dropped to zero at 03:10 and stayed there, and patchy floc was first noted on the next round, matching the failure time.
clueText.nc-b: Last month the jar tests were normal, which only confirms the dose was right before the failure.
clueText.nc-c: The monthly summary cannot pinpoint a failure that began this shift.

tasks.prompt: One of two parallel flocculation trains at a Manitoba plant produces poor settled water while the other train, on the same raw water and dose, performs normally.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional western Canadian Class 2 water plant case: steady plant flow unless noted, archived plant and laboratory records available for review, and provincial drinking water requirements and the Guidelines for Canadian Drinking Water Quality apply in general terms.

evidence.label: Train 2 settled turbidity is 1.2 NTU and Train 1 is 4.3 NTU at the same flow in each train.
Both trains receive the same coagulated water from a common rapid mix.
The Train 1 flocculator motor runs, but the paddle shaft does not rotate when watched through the hatch.
Floc leaving Train 1 is small and unformed, and floc leaving Train 2 is large and settles well.
A coupling guard on the Train 1 drive was found warm, with rubber dust beneath it.

inference.prompt: Which explanation is best supported by the observations?

options.label: The alum dose is wrong for the raw water
Train 1 is hydraulically overloaded compared with Train 2
The Train 1 clarifier blanket has risen and is washing out
The Train 1 flocculator drive coupling has failed, so that train gets no gentle mixing

inference.explanation: Both trains share dose and raw water and carry the same flow, yet only Train 1 fails, its paddle shaft does not turn while the motor runs, and there is rubber dust at the coupling. Dose and overload are common or equal, and no blanket observation is offered.

nextClue.prompt: Which archived record best confirms the coupling failure point?

options.label: Archived flow split records for the two trains
Archived drive inspection and vibration notes for the Train 1 flocculator
Archived common rapid mix dose log

nextClue.explanation: Archived drive inspection and vibration notes for the Train 1 flocculator directly records the condition behind the keyed explanation over time, so it best confirms it against the alternatives.

clueText.nc-a: Flow split records show an even split all week, which removes overload from consideration.
clueText.nc-b: Notes from last month flagged rising vibration and coupling wear on Train 1 and recommended replacement, which was deferred.
clueText.nc-c: The dose log is steady and shared by both trains, so it cannot explain a one train failure.

tasks.prompt: Sweep floc is poor and settled turbidity is high at a plant that doses lime with alum, and staff report a slippery feel at the plant tap.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional western Canadian Class 2 water plant case: steady plant flow unless noted, archived plant and laboratory records available for review, and provincial drinking water requirements and the Guidelines for Canadian Drinking Water Quality apply in general terms.

evidence.label: Coagulation pH reads 8.8, well above the plant target range of 6.8 to 7.4.
Raw alkalinity is normal, but treated alkalinity has risen to 165 mg/L as CaCO3.
The lime feeder runs continuously, including during a period when the control signal called for it to stop.
Jar tests at pH 7.1 form large sweep floc and settle to 1.2 NTU at the current alum dose.
Alum dose and raw turbidity have not changed.

inference.prompt: Which explanation is best supported by the observations?

options.label: Lime is being overfed, pushing pH above the range where alum forms good sweep floc
Alum is being underfed for the raw load
The raw water has turned cold and slowed flocculation
The rapid mixer has failed and coagulant is not dispersing

inference.explanation: pH is far above target, treated alkalinity climbed, the lime feeder runs when it should be stopped, and jars at normal pH settle well on the same alum dose. Alum dose and temperature are unchanged, and a dispersion failure would not raise alkalinity.

nextClue.prompt: Which archived record best confirms the lime feeder control fault?

options.label: Archived raw water temperature log
Archived alum day tank level record
Archived lime feeder output signal and run time log

nextClue.explanation: Archived lime feeder output signal and run time log directly records the condition behind the keyed explanation over time, so it best confirms it against the alternatives.

clueText.nc-a: Raw temperature stayed near 12 C, which does not explain a pH of 8.8.
clueText.nc-b: Alum tank drawdown matches the set dose, which clears the alum feed.
clueText.nc-c: The log shows the feeder at full output for 26 hours, including 9 hours when the controller output was zero, confirming a stuck feeder control.

tasks.prompt: A lime softening plant in Saskatchewan finds white deposits forming in its finished water pumps each time a second solids contact unit is brought online.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional western Canadian Class 2 water plant case: steady plant flow unless noted, archived plant and laboratory records available for review, and provincial drinking water requirements and the Guidelines for Canadian Drinking Water Quality apply in general terms.

evidence.label: With both units online, total flow per unit falls to about half the design rate and sludge blanket solids climb well above the normal range.
Finished water from the two unit operation carries fine white solids that settle slowly in a sample bottle.
With one unit online at full rate, deposits stop and finished turbidity is low.
Lime and soda ash doses per megalitre are the same in both modes.
The deposits analyse as calcium carbonate.

inference.prompt: Which explanation is best supported by the observations?

options.label: The second unit is contaminated with scale
Running both units at half rate thickens the blankets until precipitated solids carry over, while the single unit at design rate keeps its blanket stable
The lime dose doubles when the second unit starts
The pumps cavitate with two units online

inference.explanation: Deposits are calcium carbonate, they appear only in the two unit half rate mode at unchanged dose per megalitre, and blanket solids climb in that mode. Carryover from over thickened blankets fits, not contamination, dose or cavitation.

nextClue.prompt: Which archived record best confirms the operating mode effect?

options.label: Archived blanket solids and finished turbidity records by operating mode
Archived lime dose records
Archived pump inspection reports

nextClue.explanation: Archived blanket solids and finished turbidity records by operating mode directly records the condition behind the keyed explanation over time, so it best confirms it against the alternatives.

clueText.nc-a: Records show carryover episodes only in two unit mode across a year, with blanket solids high in every episode.
clueText.nc-b: Dose per megalitre is flat across both modes.
clueText.nc-c: Pump inspections show wear following, not preceding, the deposit episodes.

tasks.prompt: During spring snowmelt in the Alberta foothills, floc became pinpoint and settled turbidity rose, even though the soda ash feeder is running and delivering at its usual rate.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional western Canadian Class 2 water plant case: steady plant flow unless noted, archived plant and laboratory records available for review, and provincial drinking water requirements and the Guidelines for Canadian Drinking Water Quality apply in general terms.

evidence.label: Raw alkalinity has fallen from 95 mg/L to 34 mg/L as CaCO3 as dilute snowmelt entered the creek source.
Coagulation pH drops to 6.0 after alum addition, from a raw pH of 7.4.
Jar tests with extra soda ash added restore pH 7.0 and settle to 1.4 NTU at the current alum dose.
A feeder drawdown test confirms soda ash is delivering at its set rate, but the set rate was sized for the old raw alkalinity.
Raw turbidity is only moderately higher than usual.

inference.prompt: Which explanation is best supported by the observations?

options.label: The soda ash feeder has failed mechanically
The alum dose is excessive and restabilizing particles
Snowmelt dilution cut raw alkalinity so the usual alkalinity feed rate no longer replaces what alum consumes
The clarifier is hydraulically overloaded

inference.explanation: The feeder passes its drawdown test, raw alkalinity collapsed with snowmelt, pH falls on alum addition, and jars recover with extra alkalinity. The feed rate, not the feeder, is undersized for the new source chemistry, and no overload or jar overdose pattern is shown.

nextClue.prompt: Which archived record best confirms the snowmelt alkalinity pattern?

options.label: Archived raw alkalinity and creek flow records from past snowmelt periods
Archived soda ash feeder repair invoices
Archived clarifier flow records

nextClue.explanation: Archived raw alkalinity and creek flow records from past snowmelt periods directly records the condition behind the keyed explanation over time, so it best confirms it against the alternatives.

clueText.nc-a: Past snowmelts show the same alkalinity collapse as creek flow rose, and settled turbidity recovered each time the soda ash rate was raised.
clueText.nc-b: Repair invoices are old and the feeder just passed a drawdown test.
clueText.nc-c: Clarifier flows stayed within the normal spring range.

tasks.prompt: Settled turbidity at a British Columbia plant is excellent at 0.9 NTU, yet treated water organic removal has fallen and disinfection byproduct formation in distribution samples is trending up.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional western Canadian Class 2 water plant case: steady plant flow unless noted, archived plant and laboratory records available for review, and provincial drinking water requirements and the Guidelines for Canadian Drinking Water Quality apply in general terms.

evidence.label: Jar tests at the current coagulation pH of 7.3 remove turbidity well but remove only about 25 percent of dissolved organic carbon.
The same jar series run at pH 5.9 removes about 55 percent of dissolved organic carbon with similar settled turbidity.
Raw dissolved organic carbon is 5.8 mg/L and raw turbidity is low at 6 NTU.
Alum dose is at the usual turbidity based setting and has not been adjusted for organics.
Filter performance and chlorine residual at the plant are normal.

inference.prompt: Which explanation is best supported by the observations?

options.label: The filters are passing organic matter through media defects
Coagulation is optimized for turbidity at a pH too high for good organics removal, so dissolved organics pass through
The chlorine dose is too low and is creating the byproduct trend
The alum stock is diluted

inference.explanation: Jars show the same dose at lower pH removes twice the dissolved organics with no turbidity penalty, while filters and residuals are normal. The process is tuned for turbidity, not organics. Diluted alum would hurt turbidity removal too, and low chlorine would lower, not raise, byproduct formation.

nextClue.prompt: Which archived record best confirms the pH dependent organics pattern?

options.label: Archived paired jar test records of dissolved organic carbon removal against coagulation pH
Archived filter media inspection report
Archived chlorine dose log

nextClue.explanation: Archived paired jar test records of dissolved organic carbon removal against coagulation pH directly records the condition behind the keyed explanation over time, so it best confirms it against the alternatives.

clueText.nc-a: Archived jars across three seasons show organics removal rising steadily as coagulation pH drops toward 6, at constant dose.
clueText.nc-b: The media inspection found the beds in good condition.
clueText.nc-c: The chlorine dose log is steady, so a dose change does not explain the trend.

tasks.prompt: Floc leaving the first flocculation stage at a Saskatchewan plant is large and healthy, but by the last stage it is broken into small fragments and settled turbidity has risen.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional western Canadian Class 2 water plant case: steady plant flow unless noted, archived plant and laboratory records available for review, and provincial drinking water requirements and the Guidelines for Canadian Drinking Water Quality apply in general terms.

evidence.label: Flocculator speed in the last stage was raised during maintenance last week and left at the higher setting.
Floc sampled after stage one is large and settles quickly, while floc after the last stage is fragmented.
A bench test stirring a formed floc sample at the new last stage speed breaks it into the same small fragments.
Alum dose, raw turbidity and alkalinity are unchanged.
Settled turbidity was 1.5 NTU before the maintenance visit and is now 3.8 NTU.

inference.prompt: Which explanation is best supported by the observations?

options.label: The alum dose has become too low
The higher last stage mixing speed is shearing floc after it forms
The clarifier blanket is washing out
Cold water is slowing floc formation

inference.explanation: Floc forms well in stage one and fragments only after the stage whose speed was raised, and the bench test reproduces the breakage at that speed. Formation problems from dose or cold would appear at stage one, and no blanket rise is observed.

nextClue.prompt: Which archived record best confirms the speed change effect?

options.label: Archived flocculator speed settings before and after the maintenance visit, with settled turbidity
Archived sludge blanket surveys
Archived raw water temperature log

nextClue.explanation: Archived flocculator speed settings before and after the maintenance visit, with settled turbidity directly records the condition behind the keyed explanation over time, so it best confirms it against the alternatives.

clueText.nc-a: Settings show the last stage speed doubled at the visit and settled turbidity stepped up the same day, reversing a month of stable results.
clueText.nc-b: Blanket surveys stayed in the normal band through the change.
clueText.nc-c: Raw temperature changed by only 1 C that week.

tasks.prompt: A plant manager blames coagulation for poor settled turbidity, but the jar tests run by the day shift look excellent.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional western Canadian Class 2 water plant case: steady plant flow unless noted, archived plant and laboratory records available for review, and provincial drinking water requirements and the Guidelines for Canadian Drinking Water Quality apply in general terms.

evidence.label: Jar tests at the plant dose settle to 1.1 NTU and floc entering the clarifier is large and settles well in a cylinder test.
Dye added at the clarifier inlet appears at the effluent weir in about 20 minutes against a theoretical detention time near 3 hours.
Most of the basin surface is calm, with a visible fast stream running from inlet to outlet along one side.
The inlet baffle was found tilted and partly detached during a basin inspection last week.
Flow, dose and sludge blanket depth are all in their normal ranges.

inference.prompt: Which explanation is best supported by the observations?

options.label: The sludge blanket has risen and is washing over the weir
The coagulant dose is too low to form settleable floc
The basin is hydraulically overloaded beyond its design flow
Water is short-circuiting through the basin because the damaged inlet baffle lets a jet stream straight to the outlet

inference.explanation: Dye crosses in 20 minutes against a 3 hour theoretical time, a fast side stream is visible, the inlet baffle is damaged, and floc settles well in a cylinder. Blanket, dose and flow are all recorded normal or proven good by the cylinder test.

nextClue.prompt: Which archived record best confirms the short-circuit path?

options.label: Archived sludge blanket survey
Archived plant flow records
Archived dye tracer study results for this basin

nextClue.explanation: Archived dye tracer study results for this basin directly records the condition behind the keyed explanation over time, so it best confirms it against the alternatives.

clueText.nc-a: The blanket survey shows a normal, even blanket, which clears sludge washout.
clueText.nc-b: Flow records confirm operation within design flow all week.
clueText.nc-c: The tracer study shows a sharp early peak at 18 minutes and a long tail, the classic short-circuit pattern for this basin.

tasks.prompt: At a Yukon community plant in February, settled turbidity is poor and the operator reports the flocculation basin feels sluggish, with visible ice along the basin walls.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional western Canadian Class 2 water plant case: steady plant flow unless noted, archived plant and laboratory records available for review, and provincial drinking water requirements and the Guidelines for Canadian Drinking Water Quality apply in general terms.

evidence.label: Raw water temperature is 0.5 C and the flocculator drive oil was last changed three years ago.
The flocculator paddle speed measures about half its nameplate speed, and the gearbox oil is thick and dark.
Jar tests stirred at full paddle speed in the heated lab form good floc, while jars stirred at the measured basin speed form poor floc in the same time.
Alum dose, raw turbidity, pH and alkalinity match the plant winter targets.
After the gearbox was warmed during a test, paddle speed rose partway toward nameplate.

inference.prompt: Which explanation is best supported by the observations?

options.label: The alum dose is too low for winter water
Cold thickened gearbox oil has slowed the flocculator, cutting the mixing the floc needs
The rapid mixer is dispersing coagulant unevenly
The clarifier ice is channelling flow to the outlet

inference.explanation: Paddle speed is half of nameplate, the oil is old and thick, warming the gearbox raises speed, and jars at full speed succeed where jars at basin speed fail. Dose and chemistry are on target, and the jar comparison isolates mixing speed rather than flow channelling.

nextClue.prompt: Which archived record best confirms the drive maintenance link?

options.label: Archived flocculator drive maintenance and paddle speed check records
Archived clarifier ice survey
Archived alum dose log

nextClue.explanation: Archived flocculator drive maintenance and paddle speed check records directly records the condition behind the keyed explanation over time, so it best confirms it against the alternatives.

clueText.nc-a: Records show speed checks falling each winter since the oil change was skipped, with recovery the one winter the oil was changed on schedule.
clueText.nc-b: The ice survey shows wall ice only, with the basin centre open.
clueText.nc-c: The dose log matches the winter target all season.

tasks.prompt: A chlorine contact tank at a British Columbia plant shows a comfortable theoretical detention time of 60 minutes, yet the operator doubts the plant is earning the CT credit it claims.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional western Canadian Class 2 water plant case: steady plant flow unless noted, archived plant and laboratory records available for review, and provincial drinking water requirements and the Guidelines for Canadian Drinking Water Quality apply in general terms.

evidence.label: A step dose tracer test gives a T10 time of 14 minutes at the normal operating flow.
The tracer curve shows a sharp peak in the first few minutes and a long low tail.
One of three baffle curtains in the tank was found torn and hanging loose during inspection.
Chlorine residual at the outlet is steady and the dose has not changed.
Tank inlet and outlet are at opposite ends with no other visible damage.

inference.prompt: Which explanation is best supported by the observations?

options.label: The chlorine dose is too low for the water demand
The tank is short-circuiting through the torn baffle, so the effective contact time is the T10 of 14 minutes, not the theoretical 60
The outlet residual analyser has drifted low
The tracer chemical reacted with chlorine and disappeared early

inference.explanation: The tracer T10 is a quarter of the theoretical time with an early sharp peak, and a baffle curtain is torn. Residual is steady, so dose is not the issue, and a reacting tracer would shrink the whole curve rather than produce an early peak and long tail.

nextClue.prompt: Which archived record best confirms the contact tank flow pattern?

options.label: Archived tracer study reports from commissioning and from this year
Archived chlorine dose log
Archived residual analyser calibration record

nextClue.explanation: Archived tracer study reports from commissioning and from this year directly records the condition behind the keyed explanation over time, so it best confirms it against the alternatives.

clueText.nc-a: The commissioning tracer gave a T10 of 44 minutes with baffles intact, and this year the T10 fell to 14 minutes, matching the torn curtain.
clueText.nc-b: The dose log is steady through both tracer studies.
clueText.nc-c: The analyser calibrated within tolerance last week.

tasks.prompt: In January at a Manitoba plant, the calculated disinfection performance fell short even though the chlorine residual at the clearwell outlet is the same as in summer.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional western Canadian Class 2 water plant case: steady plant flow unless noted, archived plant and laboratory records available for review, and provincial drinking water requirements and the Guidelines for Canadian Drinking Water Quality apply in general terms.

evidence.label: Water temperature is 2 C, down from 18 C in summer.
Clearwell outlet pH is 8.4, up from 7.4 in summer after a softening change.
Free chlorine residual is 0.9 mg/L in both seasons and contact time is unchanged.
Reference CT tables in the plant manual require much higher CT at low temperature and high pH for the same inactivation.
Tracer testing last fall confirmed the baffling factor used in the calculation.

inference.prompt: Which explanation is best supported by the observations?

options.label: The residual analyser reads lower in cold water
Cold temperature and high pH together reduce chlorine effectiveness, so the same residual and time no longer deliver the required CT
The clearwell volume shrank over the winter
Ammonia in the source is converting free chlorine to combined chlorine

inference.explanation: Residual, time and baffling are verified unchanged, while temperature fell and pH rose, the two conditions the CT tables penalize. No analyser, volume or ammonia observation supports the other options.

nextClue.prompt: Which archived record best confirms the seasonal CT pattern?

options.label: Archived monthly CT calculation sheets with temperature and pH for two years
Archived clearwell level records
Archived raw ammonia results

nextClue.explanation: Archived monthly CT calculation sheets with temperature and pH for two years directly records the condition behind the keyed explanation over time, so it best confirms it against the alternatives.

clueText.nc-a: The sheets show the CT shortfall appearing every winter as temperature falls and worsening after the pH change, at constant residual.
clueText.nc-b: Clearwell levels run in the same band in both seasons.
clueText.nc-c: Raw ammonia has been below detection in every sample.

tasks.prompt: CT compliance at a Saskatchewan plant is marginal on weekday mornings but comfortable at midday, with the same chlorine dose and residual target all day.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional western Canadian Class 2 water plant case: steady plant flow unless noted, archived plant and laboratory records available for review, and provincial drinking water requirements and the Guidelines for Canadian Drinking Water Quality apply in general terms.

evidence.label: Plant flow peaks at 210 L/s between 07:00 and 09:00 and runs near 110 L/s at midday.
A tracer test run at peak flow gave a T10 about half the T10 measured at midday flow.
Outlet free chlorine residual holds near 0.8 mg/L at both times.
The CT calculation sheet in use applies the midday T10 value to the whole day.
Temperature and pH change little through the day.

inference.prompt: Which explanation is best supported by the observations?

options.label: Chlorine demand rises in the morning and consumes the residual
The morning calculation overstates CT because it uses the midday contact time instead of the shorter peak flow T10
The clearwell baffles fail only at high level
Operators are sampling the residual at the wrong location in the morning

inference.explanation: Residual, temperature and pH hold steady, but tracer T10 halves at peak flow while the sheet uses the midday value all day. The error is the contact time input, not demand, baffles or sampling location.

nextClue.prompt: Which archived record best confirms the flow dependent contact time?

options.label: Archived tracer results at low, medium and peak flows for the contact tank
Archived hourly chlorine demand tests
Archived sample location audit

nextClue.explanation: Archived tracer results at low, medium and peak flows for the contact tank directly records the condition behind the keyed explanation over time, so it best confirms it against the alternatives.

clueText.nc-a: The archived series shows T10 falling steadily as flow rises, with the peak flow value near half the midday value used on the sheet.
clueText.nc-b: Hourly demand tests show demand flat through the morning.
clueText.nc-c: The audit confirmed the sample tap location last quarter.

tasks.prompt: A contact tank at an Alberta plant has slowly lost effective volume over two years, and recent tracer results are worse than the commissioning results.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional western Canadian Class 2 water plant case: steady plant flow unless noted, archived plant and laboratory records available for review, and provincial drinking water requirements and the Guidelines for Canadian Drinking Water Quality apply in general terms.

evidence.label: A drained inspection found 0.6 m of settled solids covering the tank floor, in a tank 3 m deep.
The tracer T10 has fallen from 38 minutes at commissioning to 26 minutes at the same flow.
Inlet turbidity to the tank has run slightly high during spring runoff each year.
Chlorine dose, residual and flow are similar to commissioning conditions.
No baffle damage was found during the inspection.

inference.prompt: Which explanation is best supported by the observations?

options.label: The baffles have deteriorated and are short-circuiting the tank
Accumulated solids have displaced about a fifth of the tank volume, cutting the real contact time
The tracer method changed and the results are not comparable
The chlorine injection point was moved

inference.explanation: Solids occupy about a fifth of the depth, baffles are intact, conditions match commissioning, and T10 fell in step with the buildup. The displaced volume explains the loss without baffle or method changes.

nextClue.prompt: Which archived record best confirms the volume loss timeline?

options.label: Archived tank cleaning and inspection records with solids depth measurements
Archived baffle inspection photographs
Archived chlorine injection drawings

nextClue.explanation: Archived tank cleaning and inspection records with solids depth measurements directly records the condition behind the keyed explanation over time, so it best confirms it against the alternatives.

clueText.nc-a: Records show solids depth growing from a thin layer to 0.6 m over two years with no cleaning, tracking the falling T10 values.
clueText.nc-b: Photographs show the baffles intact at each inspection.
clueText.nc-c: The injection drawings are unchanged since commissioning.
